transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-17 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lin (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions), Evan Holt (Montague Head of ML), Priya Desai (Infra Lead), Mark Reynolds (CTO), Sara Kim (PM)

[00:00:00] Maya Lin: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate the time. quick agenda — understand your workload, cost constraints, and talk through levers we have at Redwood for lowering unit economics: batching, caching, quant, and hosting mix. then capture next steps.

[00:00:25] Evan Holt: yeah thanks Maya. um we run a ML inference platform for grid-optimization and some customer-facing analytics. big constraint is predictable spend— we have quarter budgets, can't spike past a hard cap. latency SLO is, like, 120ms p50 for small prompts, 800ms p95 for 2–4k token flows.

[00:00:48] Maya Lin: ok got it. and can you, uh, tell us current stack? where are you hosting models today?

[00:00:55] Evan Holt: mostly in house on k8s, mixed GPU fleet — 40% A100 style, some older ones. We use a 3rd-party inference layer but it's pretty manual so utilization is low. want to compare hosted Redwood vs reserved dedicated vs private V P C install.

[00:01:20] Carlos Ruiz: hi, I'm Carlos. quick follow up — typical prompt lengths and qps? and are requests batched client-side?

[00:01:27] Sara Kim: most calls are short: 20–80 tokens for realtime alerts, but we have a 10% tail that are long conversations, like 2–5k tokens for incident summarization. QPS is bursty: baseline ~40 qps, spikes up to 900 qps for 3–5 minutes during grid events.

[00:01:55] Priya Desai: budget is basically a fixed monthly allocation. if we go hosted and hit spikes we need hard throttle or fast fallback to smaller models. we also prefer single-tenant for some internal workloads.

[00:02:12] Mark Reynolds: security is a check — SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs — we can get into that later. first is the economics.

[00:02:21] Maya Lin: yeah makes sense. ok let's, uh, talk about per-token pricing. for hosted, you're billed per generated token + input tokens. we also provide quantization profiles and batching suggestions — tradeoff is latency vs cost. typical rule of thumb: if you can increase batching from 1 to 8 you get 3x-5x token throughput improvement, but tail latency can increase.

[00:02:50] Evan Holt: 3x-5x is quite broad. can you give a more concrete example for like a 4k seq model?

[00:02:58] Carlos Ruiz: sure. for a 4k model on an Llama-ish backbone on an A100-like machine, single-request latency might be 600–800ms. if you enable continuous batching with small windows (30–50ms) and batch size of 8, throughput per GPU improves ~3.2x and effective cost per token drops accordingly. if you need strict p95 latency under 900ms, we can tune— smaller batching windows, prefix KV caching, and lower-precision kernels. but cost goes up as latency constraints tighten.

[00:03:33] Priya Desai: pv caching? you mean KV cache? how reliable are cache hits across our workload?

[00:03:40] Carlos Ruiz: yes K V cache — sorry, transcription slip. For conversational sessions where prefix repeats (like system messages + user context), a lot of tokens are reused; hit rates can be 40–70% depending on prompt variability. for one-off summarization, lower. we can instrument per-route cache hit estimation in the pilot.

[00:04:00] Sara Kim: can Redwood fall back to smaller models automatically during a spike? we want to prioritize critical alerts with low cost during spikes.

[00:04:07] Maya Lin: yeah that's a common pattern — policy-based routing. we can set a spike guard: route critical routes to primary (low-latency, higher-cost) and default to a cheaper model when bursting beyond threshold. cost management plus SLOs.

[00:04:22] Mark Reynolds: ok, how predictable is dedicated? we need to know if monthly reserved capacity smooths out cost variance.

[00:04:29] Carlos Ruiz: Dedicated gives far more predictability — reserved GPU pools. you pay for capacity, not per token, but we help map expected token volume to commit levels. for high sustained loads it usually lowers unit cost. downside: you still want overflow handling for spikes — we offer burst-to-hosted and cross-region fallback.

[00:04:52] Evan Holt: burst-to-hosted — so a hybrid mix. how's billing done if we burst from dedicated to hosted? do you prorate?

[00:04:58] Maya Lin: billing is additive: committed capacity is billed monthly; hosted on top is billed per-token during bursts. we can set thresholds and alerts to avoid surprises. we also provide per-token estimates in our pilot spreadsheet so you can model scenarios.

[00:05:14] Priya Desai: what's the granularity of the batching config? can we control windows per route?

[00:05:20] Carlos Ruiz: yes per-route batching windows, max batch, and latency SLOs. plus automatic cache and KV retention policies per model route. We recommend measuring your request time distribution first; if most requests are <100 tokens, aggressive batching helps. if tail is long, consider separate route for long sessions with different batching.

[00:05:43] Evan Holt: quantization — will that affect hallucinations for our summarization tasks? we care about fidelity.

[00:05:49] Priya Nair: quantization lowers precision but the impact varies. we have vetted quant profiles for many open models — often 4-bit or mixed 8-bit gives 20–40% throughput improvement with minimal quality regression for classification and many summarization tasks. we recommend evals on your prompt set during pilot.

[00:06:10] Sara Kim: how long does a bench run take? like a hosted micro-benchmark to project unit cost?

[00:06:16] Carlos Ruiz: a focused micro-bench with representative prompts and a few hundred to a few thousand requests takes 2–3 hours to run including setup; full evals with quality regressions take longer. we can do a hosted bench first to get quick numbers, then mirror the same config on dedicated for a delta comparison.

[00:06:33] Evan Holt: on data residency — some workloads must stay in our VPC. for those we'd need Redwood Private. what's the delta in setup time?

[00:06:39] Maya Lin: Private (V P C/on-prem) typically takes longer — a few weeks for a standard deployment with our package and integrations, longer if air-gapped or compliant environments. cost model is license + infra + support; it's predictable but upfront. For mixed workloads, many customers run private for sensitive routes and hosted for public-facing features.

[00:06:58] Priya Desai: ok, that matches our thinking. one more on caching — if we get 50% cache hit rate on the 10% of long conversation traffic, what delta do we see in dollars?

[00:07:08] Carlos Ruiz: rough math: if long-tail accounts for 10% of tokens but you hit 50% via KV, effective token count from that slice halves. overall burn reduces by about 5% in that simplified model. but combined with batching on short requests you can get much larger overall reductions. we'll put exact scenarios in the pricing workbook.

[00:07:29] Mark Reynolds: competitors — we ran some tests vs Hyperserve and Anthropic. they beat us on throughput in some configs, but Redwood's routing, KV caching and fallbacks were attractive. any specifics we should be aware of?

[00:07:45] Maya Lin: Hyperserve tends to optimize for single-model throughput but has less flexible routing. Anthropic's managed endpoints are simple but cost can be opaque. Redwood focuses on observability and deterministic unit economics — you can see per-token and per-route cost and where cache/batching contributed.

[00:08:05] Sara Kim: what metrics will you surface in the pilot?

[00:08:09] Carlos Ruiz: per-route tokens in/out, cache hits, average batch size, per-batch latency distribution, GPU utilization, and per-token cost estimate. also we export traces for debugging.

[00:08:22] Evan Holt: response: ok that covers tech. what about contract length for dedicated commitments?

[00:08:29] Maya Lin: standard is 12-month or 36-month reserved commits; discounts increase with term and committed capacity. we often start with a 3–6 month pilot on hosted then convert to dedicated commit informed by observed utilization.

[00:08:44] Priya Desai: can we have hard budget caps enforced so we don't exceed monthly allocation?

[00:08:49] Maya Lin: yes — budget controls, rate limits, and automated fallbacks. we can push alerts at 70/85/95% and switch non-critical routes to cheaper models automatically.

[00:08:59] Mark Reynolds: good. ok let's recap and next steps.

[00:09:03] Maya Lin: recap: Redwood to provide pilot pricing workbook with hosted vs dedicated scenarios; Carlos to share micro-bench checklist and run a hosted micro-bench; customer to provide traffic histogram and SLOs; schedule bench week of 2026-06-29.

[00:09:15] Evan Holt: yep we'll get that by Monday the 22nd.

[00:09:18] Maya Lin: perfect. any final questions?

[00:09:22] Sara Kim: just one — do you have a short security pack for private installs we can share with legal?

[00:09:27] Priya Nair: yes, I'll include SOC2, SAML docs, KMS integration notes and typical network diagrams in the follow-up email.

[00:09:35] Mark Reynolds: ok thanks everyone.

[00:09:38] Maya Lin: thank you all, we'll follow up with materials.

[00:09:42] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-said acronyms (V P C, K V cache), filler words captured, some technical shorthand.
